chapters.relation: LaRocca's introduction frames the whole volume through Plato's ancient 'quarrel between philosophy and poetry' and his critique of mimesis (Republic Book X), arguing that documentary film is just another kind of poetic imitation whose truth-claims deserve philosophical scrutiny. Drawing on Cavell's 'film was as if made for philosophy,' Kiarostami's 'cinema is nothing but fakery,' Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' and Flaherty's 'sometimes you have to lie to tell the truth,' he shows how documentary blurs fiction/nonfiction and courts fabrication. He reads the digital turn (Manovich, Rodowick) as pushing cinema toward Baudrillard's hyperreal simulacra, images that no longer index reality but simulate it.

Cavell argues that photography's power expresses the mind's fall into skepticism about the external world, reading film as 'a moving image of skepticism' since we see things present to us that are not actually before us. Interpreting Capra's Mr. Deeds Goes to Town, he treats Gary Cooper's Deeds defending his 'fidgetiness' as thinking as a popular-cinema reenactment of Descartes's cogito: after Emerson, who says we can no longer say 'I think, I am' for ourselves, the proof of existence shifts from the mind's self-certainty to the live body's visible restlessness caught by the camera. He links the fidgeting body to Heidegger's das Man and Nietzsche's last man, and invokes Wittgenstein and Emerson on our being 'away' from the world.

Carroll offers a critical reconstruction of Andre Bazin's film theory, separating Bazin's lasting achievement as a historian of film style from his dubious metaphysical commitments. He shows how Bazin championed 'spatial realism'—deep-focus, long-take sequence shots as in Renoir's Rules of the Game and Welles's Citizen Kane—against Soviet and Hollywood montage, on the grounds that unedited homogeneous space imparts authenticity, grants the spectator freedom to discover meaning, and preserves the ambiguity of reality. Carroll treats Bazin's claim that recording realism is cinema's essential destiny as an anti-realist target to be demythologized, defending the study of film-realist style while rejecting the essentialist evolutionary scheme underneath it.

Currie defines documentary via the distinction between a trace (a causal, intention-independent record like a photograph, footprint, or death mask) and testimony (an intention-mediated representation like a painting or written history), placing simulations between them. A film is an ideal documentary when its images' 'trace content' coheres with its narrative, whereas Casablanca or All the President's Men has a separate 'narrative content' representing fictional characters. He grades real cases—Night Mail's faked mail-sorting, Roger and Me's rearranged chronology, Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will—by degree of coherence, and argues trace content is nonconceptual while narrative content is conceptual, so most docudramas are really fictions.

Plantinga attacks subjectivist theories that locate the fiction/nonfiction distinction solely 'in the mind of the audience,' using the fable of a naive student, Michael, who takes such theories literally and cites Star Wars and E.T. as sources in a history paper on space travel. Against Branigan and Eitzen ('When is a documentary?'), he argues you cannot legitimately comprehend a fiction film nonfictionally because that confuses a document with a documentary. He proposes a three-part account: the distinction resides in cultural convention, in the film's designed features, and in the viewer's reception, hinging on the filmmaker's 'assertive stance' versus 'fictive stance'—like the difference between a screwdriver and a hammer.

Sobchack offers a semiotic phenomenology of how real death is represented in documentary, arguing that death itself always exceeds and confounds indexical representation—we never see death, only dying and the corpse. Using Aries on the modern taboo-ing of natural death, Barthes on the traumatic photograph, and the Zapruder assassination footage whose frame-by-frame scrutiny yields only mystification, she shows why violent, abrupt mortification of the lived body is the most effective cinematic sign of death. Drawing on Heidegger's Being-toward-death and its deferral, Beauvoir's 'no such thing as a natural death,' and Merleau-Ponty's lived body, she classifies documentary's ethical 'gazes' at death (accidental, helpless, endangered, interventional, humane, professional) as inscriptions of the filmmaker's moral stance in an embodied ethical space.
